speaker: SPEAKER_03
transcript: That's a great question. It's when we discuss a lot, travel around, talk to a lot of schools, high school students, and certainly the perception is that this is unprecedented the amount of contention. I would argue that we've gone through cycles. You look back even at our founders. Thomas Jefferson and John Adams had some very famous battles, some very tough elections. John Quincy Adams against Andrew Jackson was brutal and a really tough time. So we have had certainly difficult times being from Illinois, having Illinois being so proud of Abraham Lincoln certainly. That was such a difficult time in our nation. So we've gone through tough times before. There's definitely contention. There is heightened animosity. But I would also say, if you dig in a little bit deeper, there are some really good relationships, good friendships, some opportunity to be working together. As I talk to my students that I get to get out and talk with quite a bit, to me it feels like there's really two groups in Washington DC. a group of leaders that lead our parties and have very important responsibility. And then there's a larger group of rank and file members of Congress who really don't have an interest in that. They just want to get something done. So leaders and kind of the role that they have part of the job is. We got to increase our numbers and decrease their numbers. And so I think things are contentious in those situations. Among rank and file members of Congress who just want to get something done, be effective, have some impact during the time of service. I think there's opportunity to connect, to talk, to get things done. And I would say, even in financial services, you look at some of the big Issues, there has been contention. They have been some partisan divide. But then as we get into a lot of the details and more focused need to address regulation and change, those are bipartisan and vast majority of the bills that have passed out of the financial services committee and then even the vast majority of bills that have passed out of the House. I think it's over 400 bills that have passed out of the House of Representatives in the last year and a half. But vast majority, 95% of them are bipartisan and many of them are unanimous coming out of the house. So it doesn't get the focus of the media where they love the blood sports stuff. But reality is you step back a little bit and there is good cooperation. people still ask me what is the greatest surprise of serving in Washington and one of my two big things I talk about one is the vastness of bureaucracy that is a surprise still when you stand in Capitol Hill and look in literally every direction it's government as far as you can see so that's still a surprise still a challenge to work through that the other surprise for me is the quality of people I get to work with that there really are great people who are trying to do the right thing, come from maybe very different areas than I come from, have a different perspective. That's okay. There's a level of respect there and desire to work together. And so the things I enjoy the most are those opportunities to work together. Some of the caucuses that we've got where it's completely bipartisan, where we've got to focus on an issue and we want to get something done. I'm co-chair of our FinTech Caucus. We do a lot of really good important things. I'm also a co-chairman of the STEM Education Caucus, work with Dan Lipinski, Democrat from Chicago area. I love that. Doing important work, encouraging young people to go into STEM fields, science, technology, engineering, and math. So to me, that's the fun stuff. I'm also co-chairman of our Human Rights Commission in Congress, and standing up and speaking out for people who are being abused here around the world, mistreated, that's something that I really enjoy and feel like you can still make a difference.
